newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: U.N. forum agrees to continue aid to Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. forum agrees to continue aid to Afghanistan.

text.p: Wealthy donor countries agreed on Wednesday to continue giving aid to Afghanistan despite calls from some Western nations to tie further assistance to progress on ending the civil war and relaxing strict Islamic laws.

United Nations Undersecretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs Yasushi Akashi told a news conference after a two-day U.N. aid forum in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat that the donor nations had also resolved to put aid to Afghanistan on a sounder, longer-term footing.
"A consensus has been reached that we should not provide Afghanistan with a hand-to-mouth, ad hoc assistance, but with an assistance based on sustainable, longer-term planning," he said.

Akashi added the U.N. hoped to cut down on red tape and improve aid efficiency by establishing a single coordinator for assistance. And he stressed the U.N. would strive to remain impartial between Afghanistan's many warring factions.
Reduced by 10 years of Soviet occupation and more than seven years of conflict between rival warlords to one of the world's poorest nations, Afghanistan relies heavily on foreign aid.

Some of those donors have taken a dim view of the strict Islamic law introduced by the Taleban militia which seized power in Kabul last autumn. Among the most controversial moves was barring women and girls from working or studying.

Akashi, clearly anxious to defuse any controversy, said some donors had threatened to stop financing some key projects, notably in education, if what they saw as human rights abuses were not put right.

"Some donors do not feel that they are in a position to provide funding for programmes which could not be implemented in full respect for human rights principles and other international norms and standards," he said. But he declined to name them.
A delegation of Afghan women present in Ashgabat said in a statement: "The denial of female opportunities should not be used as a justification to stop aid."
The U.N. appealed to the world community last month for a total of $133 million in aid for Afghanistan this year.
A British representative to the forum said London would provide $9-11 million. The Dutch offered $10 million. Other pledges were announced by Egypt, India, Russia and Saudi Arabia.
Japan announced its intention, pending parliamentry approval, to contribute substantially to assistance efforts.
Akashi said: "There will now be a single U.N. aid coordinator, with whom all U.N. agencies will work in a true spirit of team work."
The coordinator's activities will be closely linked to the work of local and foreign non-governmental organisations."
"In this way...we will cut down on U.N. bureaucracy and become more efficient," he said.

Getting aid through to the people who need it is a major headache in Afghanistan due to a lack of centralised government and disputes among warlords who have established their own rules over various regions.
Akashi told the news conference the U.N. hoped to cope with the problem. "We do not differentiate the distribution of aid according to the political stand taken by any faction," he said.
"Aid must be impartial. It is given on the basis of the criterion of need and suffering rather than the political stand of a local warlord," he said.
